common_name: Yellow Granex Onion (Classic Vidalia-Type Short-Day Sweet Onion)

planting.note: Start seed or set transplants in fall for a spring harvest in the Gulf South; Yellow Granex is a short-day onion requiring only about 10-12 hours of daylight to bulb, and it is the original variety behind the famous Vidalia sweet onion of Georgia.

directions: Start seed or set transplants in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a short-day onion, Yellow Granex needs the shorter day lengths of a Southern fall-to-spring growing season to bulb properly and will not perform well planted in spring in most of the country. Yellow Granex is the classic variety behind Georgia's famous Vidalia sweet onion, prized for large, flattened, golden-skinned bulbs with exceptionally mild, sweet, low-pungency flesh that develops from the low-sulfur soils and mild winters of the Deep South. It is one of the best-suited onion types for Gulf Coast gardens specifically because the region's short winter day length and mild temperatures match its bulbing requirements closely. Harvest when tops fall over and yellow, then cure carefully in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot, since sweet onions like Yellow Granex have thinner skins and shorter storage life than pungent long-day storage onions.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Vidalia Onion Production

common_name: Texas Supersweet Onion (Mild Short-Day Onion for the Gulf South)

planting.note: Start seed or set transplants in fall for a spring harvest in the Gulf South; Texas Supersweet is a short-day onion bred specifically for the mild winters and short-day length of the Texas Gulf Coast and similar regions.

directions: Start seed or set transplants in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a short-day onion, Texas Supersweet needs the shorter day lengths of a Southern fall-to-spring growing season to bulb properly. Texas Supersweet produces large, globe-shaped, pale yellow bulbs with mild, sweet flavor and low pungency, bred as a regional alternative to Georgia's Vidalia-type onions for growers in Texas and across the Gulf South. Its short-day requirement and heat tolerance make it well matched to zone 9 growing conditions, where long-day storage onion types typically fail to bulb at all. Harvest when tops fall over and yellow, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location; like other sweet onions it has a shorter storage life than pungent long-day types and is best used within a few months of harvest.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Vidalia Onion Production

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; Cabernet is a long-day (14+ hour) hybrid red onion best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylight, zones 3-7.

directions: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after hardening off, and space 4-6 inches apart. Cabernet is a long-day hybrid red onion producing large, globe-shaped bulbs with deep wine-red skin and firm, moderately pungent flesh with good color that holds up well through cooking, giving dishes an attractive red tint. It stores notably well for a red onion, holding firm in a cool, dry, well-ventilated location for several months after curing. As a long-day type, it needs the 14 or more hours of summer daylight found north of about the 35th parallel to bulb properly, making it best suited to northern and mid-latitude gardens rather than the Gulf South. Harvest when the tops fall over and begin to yellow, then cure for two to three weeks before trimming and storing.
